source: NOAA/NESDIS/STAR satellite altimetry (live) · NOAA Tides & Currents tide-gauge trends · USGS/NSIDC ice equivalents · NOAA 2022 SLR scenarios

cities.name: New Orleans / Grand Isle, LA
cities.note: Highest relative rise in the U.S. — delta subsidence plus levee-dependent, much of metro below sea level.

cities.name: Houston / Galveston, TX
cities.note: Groundwater/oil-withdrawal subsidence compounds Gulf rise; hurricane storm surge multiplier.

cities.name: Miami / Virginia Key, FL
cities.note: Porous limestone bedrock lets water up through the ground — seawalls can't stop it; <2 m elevation, dense.

cities.name: New York / The Battery, NY
cities.note: Enormous exposed population and infrastructure; Sandy showed surge-on-rise risk to transit and utilities.

cities.name: San Francisco Bay / Delta, CA
cities.note: Rise near global average, but Bay-Delta levees guard the state's water supply, SFO/OAK, and low-lying fill.

ice.name: West Antarctica (unstable sector)
ice.note: The realistically vulnerable part this millennium — Thwaites/WAIS marine-based ice.

ice.name: Greenland Ice Sheet
ice.note: BedMachine v3: 7.42 ± 0.05 m if it all melted.

ice.name: Antarctic Ice Sheet (all)
ice.note: Full Antarctic ice — the overwhelming majority of Earth's land ice.

ice.name: All land ice (everything)
ice.note: Both ice sheets + all glaciers. USGS cites ~70 m (230 ft) with every mountain glacier included.

forecast.source: NOAA 2022 Interagency Sea Level Rise Technical Report (Sweet et al. 2022); IPCC AR6 cross-reference
forecast.note: Five NOAA scenarios keyed to their 2100 global target. Paths stay close through ~2050 (~0.25-0.3 m, largely locked in) and diverge after mid-century based on emissions and ice-sheet response. IPCC AR6 SSP5-8.5 likely range for 2100 is 0.6-1.0 m, with a low-confidence high end approaching 2 m — consistent with NOAA's Intermediate-High/High.

context: Full-melt scenarios unfold over centuries to millennia, not this century. Observed rise this century is ~0.3–1 m by 2100 (up to ~2 m on high-emission, rapid-ice-loss pathways for the U.S. coast). The ice bars show the ultimate ceiling each reservoir holds, not a 2100 forecast.
